| [NOTE-555](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-555.md) | Conceptualization of the Holobiont Paradigm as It Pertains to Corals | A mini-review arguing that corals must be studied as holobionts. | [NOTE-558](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-558.md) | Phase Shifts, Herbivory, and the Resilience of Coral Reefs to Climate Change | Four roofless 25 m² cages on Orpheus Island's reef crest kept large and medium fishes out for 30 months after the 1998 bleaching, against four partial cages and four open plots. | [NOTE-571](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-571.md) | Catastrophic regime shifts in ecosystems: linking theory to observation | A review of how to tell whether an ecosystem has alternative stable states. Field patterns (jumps, multimodality, dual relationships) are suggestive and never conclusive, since a stepwise driver or a simple threshold produces them too. Experiments can come close to proof: initial-state dependence, lasting shifts after temporary disturbance, and hysteresis. Models show positive feedback must be strong enough. | Read |
| [NOTE-572](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-572.md) | Resilience and Stability of Ecological Systems | Ecological theory had equated stability with behaviour near equilibrium. Holling separates stability (return to equilibrium) from resilience (the capacity to absorb change and persist, set by the domain of attraction), shows they can trade off in lakes, forests, insects and fish, and warns that managing for constant yield can erode resilience. | Read |

| [NOTE-1211](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1211.md) | Athreya, Czuppon & Gokhale — The evolution of dependence and cohesion in incipient endosymbioses | An adaptive-dynamics model in which hosts, symbionts and host–symbiont collectives are three populations. Each partner has an "obligacy" (investment in collective rather than free-living growth) and an "adhesion" (investment in synchronized, collective reproduction). The faster-growing partner, the symbiont, becomes fully obligate first. What the host's obligacy then does depends on within-collective births and deaths: it stays, rises to full dependence, or falls to none. Obligacy rises only if the collective's carrying capacity is high enough; collective growth rate does not matter. Early on, dependence evolves ahead of cohesion. That last result holds for the trait mapping the authors chose, and their own Table S1 reverses it under the opposite mapping. The authors say the available data can neither confirm nor refute it. | Read |
| [NOTE-1212](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1212.md) | Morris, Lenski & Zinser — The Black Queen Hypothesis | Proposes that in free-living microbes, losing a costly function whose product leaks to neighbours is favoured by ordinary individual selection, and the loss runs until the remaining producers ("helpers") just supply the community, leaving most cells ("beneficiaries") dependent on a rare few. No relatedness, cooperation or collective is needed, only leakiness and frequency dependence. The one worked case is the loss of catalase-peroxidase (katG) in Prochlorococcus, which cannot survive the hydrogen peroxide that its community removes. The other cases are suggestions. | Read |
| [NOTE-1213](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1213.md) | McCutcheon, Garber, Spencer & Warren — How do bacterial endosymbionts work with so few genes? | An essay on the endosymbionts with genomes under about 200 kb, which the authors call "tipping-point endosymbionts". Below about 400 kb, symbionts almost always lose the genes to build their own envelope and to move proteins across it. Below about 200 kb, even translation erodes: ribosomal proteins, tRNAs and aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases go. Their proteomes are among the most compositionally biased in bacteria. The paper asks four questions it cannot answer: where their membranes, transporters, missing translation parts and protein stability come from. Its best guess is from the host, as in organelles. The thresholds come from a hand-picked set of genomes, and the composition analysis is called preliminary. | Read |
| [NOTE-1235](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1235.md) | Campbell et al. — Changes in endosymbiont complexity drive host-level compensatory adaptations in cicadas | In cicadas whose endosymbiont Hodgkinia has split into many lineages, each essential, the mother must put every lineage into every egg. Amplicon sequencing found every tracked Hodgkinia genotype in every egg sampled. The transmission route looks the same under the light microscope. Only M. septendecim differs significantly; the six-lineage species does not. So the compensation rests on one species. | [NOTE-1236](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1236.md) | Shigenobu, Watanabe, Hattori, Sakaki & Ishikawa — Genome sequence of the endocellular bacterial symbiont of aphids Buchnera sp. APS | The first complete genome of an obligate insect endosymbiont. Buchnera APS, from the pea aphid, has a 640,681-bp chromosome with 583 ORFs and two small plasmids. It keeps the pathways for the amino acids its host cannot make, lacks almost all of those the host can, and draws some precursors from the host, so the two partners' pathways interlock. It also lacks phospholipid and lipopolysaccharide synthesis, almost all transcriptional regulators, and recA and uvrABC. | [NOTE-1368](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1368.md) | Power et al. — What can ecosystems learn? | In a competitive Lotka–Volterra community where individual selection lowers the competitive effect ω_ij of species j on species i at a rate proportional to x_i x_j, and a normalising trade-off holds each row and column sum of ω fixed, interactions change as Hebbian learning does. In simulation (400 species, symmetric ω) the community comes to hold attractors for two past forcing patterns, completes them from fragments and switches with hysteresis. | [NOTE-1369](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1369.md) | Cooper and West — Division of labour and the evolution of extreme specialization | A kin-selection model of one cooperative trait with two phenotypes that invest q1 and q2 in helping. | [NOTE-1395](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1395.md) | Mehta, Cui, Wang and Marsland — Constrained optimization as ecological dynamics | Any minimization of f(R) over R ≥ 0 under constraints g_i(R) ≤ 0 has the KKT points of a consumer–resource dynamics as its steady states: variables are resources, each constraint is a species whose abundance is its Lagrange multiplier, and binding constraints are the surviving species. | [NOTE-1397](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1397.md) | Bunin — Ecological communities with Lotka-Volterra dynamics | For generalized Lotka–Volterra dynamics of a community assembled from a pool of S species with random interactions of mean μ/S, variance σ²/S and symmetry γ, the cavity method gives exact large-S results in the phase with a unique uninvadable fixed point: a Gaussian truncated at zero for abundances, the fraction of surviving species, and a loss of stability at σ = √2/(1 + γ) for equal carrying capacities, independent of μ. | [NOTE-1668](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1668.md) | Araki et al. — Fitness of hatchery-reared salmonids in the wild | A review of 14 studies of hatchery against wild salmonid fitness in the same habitat, nine on steelhead, and a quantitative-genetic model. Hatchery fish are generally less fit in the wild; nonlocal segregated stocks are worst (lifetime relative fitness 0.02–0.37); local wild broodstock helps but does not prevent the loss. In the authors' Hood River steelhead the loss is genetic and cumulative from the first to the second hatchery generation. Of the candidate mechanisms, relaxed selection is too slow and inbreeding would need to be too high; domestication selection is the most likely, and the model shows it can give a loss of more than 30% per generation on one trait only when selection is strong in both settings and heritability high, plausibly when it acts on several traits. | Read |

| [NOTE-1700](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1700.md) | Suding, Gross & Houseman — Alternative states and positive feedbacks in restoration ecology | A short TREE review, no data of its own. Restoring a degraded system's historical conditions or disturbance regime fails where the degraded state is held by biotic–abiotic feedbacks (invader biogeochemistry, herbivory, lost seed sources, regional change); restoration must disrupt the feedback or move the state directly, often by combined or ordered actions, and then enters a separate maintenance phase. Effect sizes are second-hand; no case tests for alternative stable states, which the authors concede is rarely possible, and none measures withdrawal after a shift. | Read |
